questions.body: What does the Java compiler do with generic type arguments (e.g. `<String>`) during compilation to bytecode?
questions.keyPoints: Type erasure removes type arguments at compile time and inserts casts where necessary.

options.text: It erases all type parameter information, replaces unbounded parameters with Object (or the first bound), and inserts casts where appropriate.
options.explanation: Java generics are implemented via Type Erasure for binary backward compatibility with pre-generic code. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> both have raw type List.

options.text: It generates a separate compiled .class file for each specialized type (reification), similar to C++ templates.
options.explanation: Java uses type erasure, not template monomorphization/reification.

options.text: It preserves type arguments in runtime heap object headers for dynamic type checking.
options.explanation: Runtime objects do not store generic type parameters.

options.text: It converts all generic collections to native C pointers.
options.explanation: Collections remain standard Java heap objects.

questions.body: According to Joshua Bloch's PECS rule, when should you use `? extends T` versus `? super T`?
questions.keyPoints: Producer Extends (reading items from the collection), Consumer Super (writing items into the collection).

options.text: Use `? extends T` when the collection produces items to be read; use `? super T` when the collection consumes items to be written.
options.explanation: PECS stands for Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super. If you only read items from a collection, it is a producer (`? extends T`). If you only write items to a collection, it is a consumer (`? super T`).

options.text: Use `? extends T` for writing data; use `? super T` for reading data.
options.explanation: This inverts the PECS principle.

options.text: Use `? extends T` for classes; use `? super T` for interfaces.
options.explanation: Both wildcards work identically with classes and interfaces.

options.text: Use `? extends T` for single threads; use `? super T` for concurrent code.
options.explanation: Wildcards are compile-time type safety mechanisms unrelated to threading.

questions.body: Given `List<? extends Number> list`, why does the compiler reject `list.add(10)`?
questions.keyPoints: The compiler cannot determine which specific subtype of Number the list holds, so it forbids adding elements.

options.text: Because the exact subtype of Number held by the list is unknown at compile time (it could be List<Double>), so the compiler cannot guarantee type safety.
options.explanation: list could refer to a List<Double> or List<Long>. Inserting an Integer (10) into a List<Double> would violate type safety. Only null is permitted.

options.text: Because 10 is an int primitive, and autoboxing does not work with wildcards.
options.explanation: Autoboxing works with generics, but the wildcard itself prohibits adding any typed element.

options.text: Because wildcards make collections read-only at the JVM bytecode level.
options.explanation: Other methods like clear() or remove() still work; adding is prohibited because the element type is open-ended.

options.text: Because Number is an abstract class.
options.explanation: Even if the bound were a concrete class (e.g., Integer), `? extends Integer` would still forbid adding elements.

questions.body: When reading an element from `List<? super Integer> list`, what is the most specific type the compiler guarantees for the retrieved element?
questions.keyPoints: Elements read from ? super Integer can only be safely typed as Object.

options.text: Object.
options.explanation: Because the list could be List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object>, the only common supertype guaranteed for any element retrieved is Object.

options.text: Integer.
options.explanation: The list might be a List<Number> containing Doubles, so assuming Integer is unsafe.

options.text: Number.
options.explanation: The list could be List<Object> containing Strings.

options.text: A compilation error occurs on any get() call on lower-bounded lists.
options.explanation: get() is completely valid; it simply returns reference type Object.

questions.body: Why does `String[] arr = new String[2]; Object[] objArr = arr; objArr[0] = 10;` throw a runtime exception, while `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); List<Object> objList = list;` fails to compile?
questions.keyPoints: Arrays in Java are covariant and check types at runtime; Generics are invariant and enforce types at compile time.

options.text: Arrays are covariant and retain runtime component type info (throwing ArrayStoreException); generics are invariant to prevent runtime corruption at compile time.
options.explanation: String[] is a subtype of Object[] (covariance), but stores its type at runtime. List<String> is NOT a subtype of List<Object> (invariance), preventing bugs at compile time.

options.text: Arrays use heap memory while Lists use stack memory.
options.explanation: Both arrays and collections reside on the heap.

options.text: Generics are covariant while arrays are invariant.
options.explanation: This reverses the definitions.

options.text: Lists only accept primitive types in Java.
options.explanation: Java collections accept object reference types, not raw primitives.

questions.body: Why does the Java compiler generate synthetic 'bridge methods' in bytecode when a class implements a parameterized interface, like `Comparable<MyClass>`?
questions.keyPoints: Bridge methods preserve polymorphism and covariant overrides after type erasure.

options.text: To preserve polymorphic method dispatch after type erasure erases the interface method parameter to Object (`compareTo(Object)` delegating to `compareTo(MyClass)`).
options.explanation: Because erasure replaces Comparable<T>.compareTo(T) with compareTo(Object), the subclass's compareTo(MyClass) would not match without a compiler-generated bridge method `compareTo(Object)`.

options.text: To bridge the execution between native JVM code and the operating system.
options.explanation: Bridge methods are purely standard bytecode methods to handle erasure polymorphism.

options.text: To allow private methods to call public methods.
options.explanation: This describes synthetic nestmate accessors, not generic bridge methods.

options.text: To serialize generic objects to JSON.
options.explanation: Bridge methods have no connection to JSON serialization.

questions.body: What is 'heap pollution' in Java, and when is it safe to use the `@SafeVarargs` annotation?
questions.keyPoints: Heap pollution occurs when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object of a different type; @SafeVarargs suppresses warnings on non-reifiable varargs.

options.text: Heap pollution occurs when a parameterized variable points to an object of a different type. @SafeVarargs can be placed on final/static methods that do not store into or leak the varargs array.
options.explanation: Because generic varargs compile to an array of Object (e.g. List<String>[]), writing to it can pollute the heap. @SafeVarargs asserts that the method only reads from the varargs array.

options.text: Heap pollution occurs when the JVM garbage collector runs out of memory; @SafeVarargs triggers an emergency GC cycle.
options.explanation: Heap pollution is a type-system integrity issue, not a low-memory event.

options.text: Heap pollution is when multiple threads access a volatile variable without synchronization.
options.explanation: That describes a concurrency race condition.

options.text: @SafeVarargs can be used on any method to automatically cast Object to T.
options.explanation: @SafeVarargs only applies to static, final, or private methods accepting varargs.

questions.body: What rule governs multiple bounds on a generic type parameter, such as `<T extends A & B & C>`?
questions.keyPoints: At most one class can be specified and it must be listed first, followed by interfaces.

options.text: At most one class can be specified, and if a class is present, it must be the first bound listed, followed by any number of interfaces.
options.explanation: Java single inheritance dictates that T can extend at most one class. Syntactically, the class must appear first: `<T extends MyClass & Interface1 & Interface2>`.

options.text: Only interfaces can be specified; classes are forbidden in multiple bounds.
options.explanation: A single class is allowed as the first bound.

options.text: Multiple classes can be listed as long as they are separated by commas instead of ampersands.
options.explanation: Java does not support multiple class inheritance.

options.text: The bounds must be listed in descending order of their package names.
options.explanation: Package names have no bearing on bound order.

questions.body: In generic frameworks (like Spring or Jackson), why is `Class<T>` used as a 'Type Token'?
questions.keyPoints: Class<T> provides runtime reified type information that would otherwise be lost to type erasure.

options.text: Because type erasure strips `T` at runtime, passing `Class<T>` provides an explicit reified type token for reflection, instantiation, or deserialization.
options.explanation: At runtime, `T.class` is invalid syntax due to erasure. Passing `Class<T> clazz` allows methods to inspect, instantiate (clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()), or cast safely.

options.text: To bypass Java bytecode verification at class loading.
options.explanation: Type tokens do not disable JVM bytecode verification.

options.text: Because Class<T> instances are stored directly in CPU L1 cache.
options.explanation: Class objects reside in standard JVM heap/metaspace memory.

options.text: To prevent other threads from garbage collecting the generic class.
options.explanation: Loaded classes are not collected as long as their ClassLoader is alive.

questions.body: Why does the Java compiler disallow direct generic array instantiation, such as `new T[10]` or `new List<String>[10]`?
questions.keyPoints: Generic array creation is disallowed because arrays are reified and generics are erased, creating type safety contradictions.

options.text: Because arrays must know and enforce their exact component type at runtime (reification), which conflicts with generic type erasure.
options.explanation: If `new List<String>[10]` were permitted, it would erase to `Object[]`. Writing `Object[] arr = listArr; arr[0] = new ArrayList<Integer>();` would break type safety without ArrayStoreException.

options.text: Because arrays cannot hold more than 100 elements when parameterized.
options.explanation: Array size limits are unrelated to types.

options.text: Because Java arrays can only hold primitive types.
options.explanation: Arrays can hold any object reference type.

options.text: Because generic types cannot be stored contiguously in memory.
options.explanation: Arrays always store references contiguously.

questions.body: Why can static fields and static methods in a class `MyClass<T>` not reference the type parameter `T`?
questions.keyPoints: Type parameter T is tied to specific instances, whereas static members belong to the class.

options.text: Because `T` is tied to an individual instance created via `new MyClass<T>()`, whereas static members are shared across all instances of raw class MyClass.
options.explanation: There is only one static copy of the class shared among MyClass<String> and MyClass<Integer>. Having a static field of type T would create ambiguity as to which T applies.

options.text: Because static members are compiled by a separate native compiler.
options.explanation: All Java code is compiled uniformly by javac.

options.text: Because static methods cannot return any value.
options.explanation: Static methods can return values, including declaring their own generic parameters: `public static <E> E method(E item)`.

options.text: Because the JVM prevents any static method from accepting parameters.
options.explanation: Static methods accept arguments normally.

questions.body: Which of the following operations involving exceptions is strictly forbidden by the Java compiler?
questions.keyPoints: A class cannot extend Throwable generically, and catch blocks cannot catch type parameters (catch (T ex)).

options.text: A class cannot directly or indirectly extend `java.lang.Throwable`, and a try-catch block cannot catch a generic type parameter (`catch (T ex)`).
options.explanation: Because type erasure strips generic types, the JVM exception handling mechanism (which depends on runtime class metadata) cannot match erased types at runtime.

options.text: A method cannot declare `throws T` in its method signature where T extends Exception.
options.explanation: `<T extends Exception> void method() throws T` is valid syntax and commonly used in type-safe exception handlers.

options.text: A catch block cannot catch an IOException.
options.explanation: Catching concrete exceptions is standard Java.

options.text: Generic methods cannot throw RuntimeExceptions.
options.explanation: Any method can throw unchecked runtime exceptions.

questions.body: What is the key difference in type safety between using `List<?>` and using raw `List`?
questions.keyPoints: List<?> is type-safe and prevents adding arbitrary objects; raw List is unchecked and allows unsafe insertions.

options.text: `List<?>` is type-safe: the compiler disallows inserting any element (except null). Raw `List` is unchecked: the compiler permits adding any object, creating risk of ClassCastException.
options.explanation: Raw types opt out of generic type checking entirely for legacy compatibility. List<?> expresses 'a list of an unknown type', preserving type safety by blocking additions.

options.text: List<?> takes twice as much memory as raw List.
options.explanation: Both compile to the same underlying raw List at bytecode level.

options.text: Raw List cannot be iterated with a foreach loop.
options.explanation: Raw lists iterate as Object.

options.text: List<?> cannot be passed as a method argument.
options.explanation: List<?> is standard syntax for generic parameters.

questions.keyPoints: Both methods have the same erasure (process(List)), causing a duplicate method signature error.

options.text: Both methods have the same erasure: `process(List)`, which violates the rule that methods in a class cannot have identical parameter signatures after erasure.
options.explanation: After type erasure, both signatures become `public void process(List list)`. Since the JVM cannot distinguish them, the compiler rejects the class.

options.text: Because String and Integer cannot both be used in the same class.
options.explanation: Any class can use both String and Integer.

options.text: Because methods named 'process' are reserved keywords in modern Java.
options.explanation: 'process' is an ordinary identifier, not a reserved keyword.

options.text: Because method overloading is prohibited when using collections.
options.explanation: Overloading is allowed if raw types differ (e.g. process(List) vs process(Set)).

questions.body: Why is a private generic helper method (e.g. `private <T> void helper(List<T> list)`) often used when implementing algorithms on wildcard types like `List<?>`?
questions.keyPoints: The helper method captures the unknown wildcard type as a concrete type variable T.

options.text: To capture the wildcard so the compiler can bind a concrete type variable `T`, enabling elements read from the list to be written back into the list.
options.explanation: With `List<?>`, list.set(0, list.get(0)) fails because the compiler cannot verify the types match. Delegating to `<T> void helper(List<T> l)` captures the wildcard as T.

options.text: To instruct the JVM to bypass garbage collection during list iteration.
options.explanation: Wildcard capture is purely a compile-time type system mechanism.

options.text: To convert the list into an array automatically.
options.explanation: No array conversion is performed.

options.text: Because wildcard methods cannot be declared public.
options.explanation: Public methods frequently use wildcard parameters (e.g., Collections.reverse(List<?>)).

questions.body: What is the purpose of a recursive type bound like `<T extends Comparable<T>>` in `public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(Collection<T> coll)`?
questions.keyPoints: Recursive bounds ensure that a type can be compared specifically to instances of its own type.

options.text: It guarantees that type `T` is comparable specifically to instances of itself, ensuring type-safe comparison without unsafe raw casts.
options.explanation: Without the recursive bound `<T extends Comparable<T>>`, an object could implement Comparable<OtherClass>, leading to runtime ClassCastException when comparing elements.

options.text: It instructs the compiler to implement the compareTo method recursively.
options.explanation: It specifies a type constraint, not a recursive algorithm.

options.text: It forces `T` to be an enum.
options.explanation: Enums use recursive bounds (`Enum<E extends Enum<E>>`), but any class like String or Integer can satisfy `<T extends Comparable<T>>`.

options.text: It permits comparing T against completely unrelated classes at runtime.
options.explanation: It restricts comparisons strictly to instances of T.

questions.body: Which of the following is a 'reifiable' type in Java whose full type information is completely available at runtime?
questions.keyPoints: Reifiable types include raw types, primitives, unbounded wildcards (List<?>), and arrays of reifiable types.

options.text: `String[]` and `List<?>`.
options.explanation: Reifiable types are those whose type information is not diminished by erasure: primitive types, non-generic classes (String), raw types (List), unbounded wildcards (`List<?>`), and arrays of reifiable types (`String[]`).

options.text: `List<String>`.
options.explanation: List<String> is non-reifiable because <String> is erased at runtime.

options.text: `Map<Integer, String>`.
options.explanation: Map<Integer, String> is non-reifiable due to type erasure.

options.text: `T` (a generic type parameter).
options.explanation: Type parameters are non-reifiable and erased to their bound.

questions.body: In Java 8+, how does the compiler determine the type parameter when invoking a generic method like `List<String> list = Collections.emptyList();`?
questions.keyPoints: Target typing and type inference deduce generic types from assignment context.

options.text: Via Target Typing / Type Inference: the compiler infers the type parameter `T = String` from the left-hand variable assignment context.
options.explanation: Java 8 enhanced target typing so generic method invocations infer their type arguments from the target type of the assignment expression without requiring explicit witness `Collections.<String>emptyList()`.

options.text: By dynamically interrogating the JVM at runtime.
options.explanation: Type inference is entirely a compile-time process.

options.text: By executing a background compilation daemon thread.
options.explanation: Standard javac compiler performs flow-sensitive type inference.

options.text: It always infers Object unless an explicit cast is added.
options.explanation: Target typing infers the specific target type (String).

questions.body: Why did Java maintain support for raw types (e.g. `List list = new ArrayList()`) when generics were introduced in Java 5?
questions.keyPoints: Raw types were retained for backward compatibility with legacy pre-Java 5 codebases.

options.text: For migration compatibility: to allow existing pre-Java 5 codebases to compile and interoperate smoothly with newer generic libraries.
options.explanation: Billions of lines of pre-Java 5 code used raw types. Disallowing them would have broken backward compatibility across the entire Java ecosystem.

options.text: Because raw types execute 5x faster than generic types on modern hardware.
options.explanation: Both compile to identical bytecode; raw types offer no performance advantage.

options.text: Because raw types are required for JPA entities.
options.explanation: JPA entities can and should use parameterized collections.

options.text: To permit storing primitive values directly without boxing.
options.explanation: Raw collections still require object references and box primitives.

questions.body: What design advantage does the self-referential generic pattern `public abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>>` provide?
questions.keyPoints: Self-referential generics enable fluent method chaining in inheritance hierarchies without unsafe casts.

options.text: It enables fluent method chaining where subclass builder methods return the exact subclass builder type rather than the base builder type.
options.explanation: In hierarchical builders, returning 'this' typed as T ensures that chained calls retain access to subclass-specific builder methods without requiring manual downcasting.

options.text: It prevents subclasses from overriding any builder methods.
options.explanation: Methods can still be overridden normally.

options.text: It forces the JVM to inline all builder methods at compile time.
options.explanation: Inlining is decided by the JIT compiler at runtime based on profiling.

options.text: It allows the builder to be used without calling build().
options.explanation: Calling build() is still needed to produce the target product.
